The Zanj revolt was purely a class revolt, not a racial struggle between Black and white people. This is clear from its social and economic conditions, from the fact that its leadership was white—its first leader, ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad, and his associates ʿAlī ibn Abān, Yaḥyā ibn Muḥammad, and Muḥammad ibn Salm—and from the fact that large groups of Bedouin Arabs and non-Zanj peasants gave valuable support by supplying its armies. See ʿAlī, p. 114; al-Ṭabarī, vol. 8, pp. 91, 95; and ʿAbd al-Fattāḥ ʿUlyān, Qarāmiṭat al-ʿIrāq, p. 24, citing Nöldeke, Sketches from Eastern History, pp. 152–153.↩︎

The name “Qarmatians” most likely comes from the man who first organized the movement and spread it in the region of Kufa, from which it later expanded into the areas where history records its presence. His name was Ḥamdān Qarmaṭ. He was a poor agricultural laborer from a village near Kufa. Around 264 AH/877 CE he came into contact with an Ismaʿili missionary known as al-Ḥusayn al-Ahwāzī, who brought him into the movement and entrusted him with spreading its message and organizing its followers in that area. The Qarmatians themselves, however, did not call their community by the name by which history came to know them. They called themselves “the believers made victorious by God, the supporters of His religion, and the reformers of the earth.” See ʿUlyān, al-Qarāmiṭa fī al-ʿIrāq, pp. 30, 35, 76.↩︎

al-Baghdādī says of the people from the tribes of southern Iraq and the Syrian desert who answered the Qarmatian call that they were proverbial for their poverty and hunger (al-Farq bayna al-Firaq, p. 142). Abū al-Faḍl, al-Ishāra fī Maḥāsin al-Tijāra, Cairo, 1318 AH, p. 43, describes the craftsmen and ordinary people in the towns who joined the movement as the poorest among the free population.↩︎

The Nabataeans were “a non-Arab people who lived between the two Iraqs. They were called Nabataeans because they drew out what the land produced; the word later came to be used for mixed groups of people and for the common population” (al-Munjid, entry “Nabaṭ”). Dr. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz al-Dūrī says that the term refers to the ancient peasants of Iraq who spoke Aramaic. After the Persians weakened them, they were absorbed among the Persians and came to identify with them. They later converted to Islam and spoke a rough form of Arabic, but kept many of their pre-Islamic traditions. Some Bedouins also settled among them, and the whole population came to be known as people of the Sawād. See al-Dūrī, Tārīkh al-ʿIrāq al-Iqtiṣādī fī al-Qarn al-Rābiʿ al-Hijrī, Baghdad, 1948, p. 26.↩︎
